html:
Sakya Monastery was founded in 1073 by Khön Könchok Gyalpo in southern Tibet, west of Shigatse, and became the seat of the Sakya school of Tibetan Buddhism. The name means "pale earth", after the grey soil of the hillside. Its heads came from the Khön family and passed the office from uncle to nephew or father to son.

In the 1240s the scholar Sakya Pandita went to the Mongol prince Köden and submitted Tibet to the Mongols, in return for a role as their go-between. His nephew Phagpa became the teacher of Kublai Khan, designed a new script for the Yuan empire and was put in charge of Buddhism across it. With Mongol backing, Sakya lamas ruled Tibet for nearly a century, until the Phagmodrupa family took over in the 1350s.

This was the first case of a lama ruling with a foreign patron, the bond of "priest and patron" later used by the Dalai Lamas with the Mongols and the Qing. The great southern monastery, a fortress-like hall built in 1268, still stands and holds a famous library.
